rules.title: Mounting of cramfs filesystems is disabled
rules.impact: Blocking the module removes the parsing code entirely instead of relying on mount policy.
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is not required on a general purpose server. The kernel module is blocked so that cramfs images cannot be mounted, intentionally or otherwise.

rules.title: Mounting of freevxfs filesystems is disabled
rules.explanation: The freevxfs file system type is a compressed, read-only Linux file system embedded in small systems (similar to cramfs). squashfs images can be used without first unpacking them.
rules.impact: Blocking the module removes the parsing code entirely instead of relying on mount policy.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem designed to succeed hfs, enabling Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem is a journaling filesystem designed for use on flash memory devices.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: OverlayFS provides a union-mount filesystem that combines an upper and lower filesystem into a single unified view. It is commonly used by container runtimes such as Docker and Podman.
rules.impact: The overlayfs module has known privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-3493 and CVE-2023-0386. Disabling unused OverlayFS support reduces the local attack surface.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem often used for LiveCD and similar images. A squashfs image can be mounted without first decompressing it.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf file system type is the Universal Disk Format used to implement the ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 specifications. It is an open-vendor file system type for storing data on a wide range of media. This file system type is required to support DVD writing and newer optical disc formats.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Restricting USB access on the system will reduce the physical attack surface of the device and reduce possible malware introduction vectors.
rules.explanation: The usb-storage kernel module enables the system to use USB mass-storage devices such as flash drives and external disks.

rules.title: Unused filesystem kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: File system kernel modules are pieces of code that can be dynamically loaded into the Linux kernel to extend its file system capabilities, the so-called operating system base kernel. File system kernel modules are typically used to add support for new hardware (as device drivers) or to add system calls.
rules.impact: Although loadable kernel filesystem modules are a convenient method of modifying a running kernel, attackers on a compromised system can abuse this to hide their processes or files, allowing them to retain control of the system. Many rootkits use loadable kernel filesystem modules in this way. Removing support for unnecessary filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary files. Placing it on a dedicated partition or tmpfs enables restrictive mount options and isolates temporary storage from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /tmp limits the impact of disk-space exhaustion through temporary files and allows protective mount options that harden a frequently abused writable location.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying nodev stops users from creating device nodes there that could be used to access hardware or bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying nosuid prevents placement of setuid binaries that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is world-writable, applying noexec reduces the risk that uploaded or staged binaries will be executed directly from temporary storage.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: /dev/shm is a shared-memory filesystem (typically tmpfs) used for inter-process communication. Mounting it separately enables restrictive mount options.
rules.impact: Isolating /dev/shm allows protective mount options that reduce abuse of shared memory as a staging area for malicious code or privilege-escalation artifacts.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /dev/shm prevents creation of device nodes in shared memory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents setuid binaries from being executed from shared memory for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm reduces the risk that shared memory will be used as an in-memory execution staging area for malicious code.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory holds user home directories and personal data. Placing it on a separate partition isolates user data from system files and supports quotas and protective mount options.
rules.impact: Isolating /home limits the impact of disk exhaustion by user data on the root filesystem and enables mount options that harden user-writable storage.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nodev prevents users from creating device nodes that could be used to access hardware or bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nosuid prevents users from creating setuid binaries in /home that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory stores variable data such as logs, caches, spools, and application state. Placing it on a separate partition isolates growth of that data from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /var reduces the risk that log or cache growth will fill the root filesystem and disrupt system services.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var prevents creation of device nodes in variable-data directories that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var prevents setuid binaries from being placed or executed under /var if write access is obtained through a compromised service.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: /var/tmp provides temporary storage that persists across reboots. Placing it on a separate partition enables restrictive mount options while isolating that storage from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/tmp limits persistence of attacker-controlled temporary files across reboots and allows protective mount options on this writable location.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/tmp prevents creation of device nodes in persistent temporary storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/tmp prevents setuid binaries from persisting across reboots in temporary storage for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/tmp reduces the risk that persistent temporary storage will be used to stage and execute malicious binaries across reboots.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory stores system and application logs. Placing it on a separate partition isolates log growth from the root filesystem and helps preserve logging capacity.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log reduces the risk that log growth will fill the root filesystem and disrupt services, and helps protect log availability for investigation.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log prevents creation of device nodes in the log directory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the log directory if write access is obtained.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log ensures the log partition remains storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted in log directories.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory stores audit daemon logs. Placing it on a separate partition isolates audit storage from other log growth and supports compliance retention.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log/audit helps preserve audit records when other logs grow rapidly and reduces the chance that audit capacity will be exhausted by unrelated logging.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log/audit prevents creation of device nodes in audit log storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log/audit prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the audit log partition.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log/audit keeps the audit partition storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted among audit logs.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: Package metadata and packages are installed only from repositories whose signatures are verified. Unsigned or third-party repositories let anyone who controls the mirror decide what is installed as root.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Package metadata and packages are installed only from repositories whose signatures are verified. Unsigned or third-party repositories let anyone who controls the mirror decide what is installed as root.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: The package provides controls the rest of the baseline depends on; it must be installed and kept current through the distribution repositories.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The latest apparmor packages are installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor provides mandatory access control (MAC).
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system installed, only the default discretionary access control system will be available.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: AppArmor is enabled for early boot by passing kernel parameters such as apparmor=1 and security=apparmor through the bootloader configuration.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled at boot, confinement profiles are not applied during system startup, leaving processes unprotected until AppArmor is activated later.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are not disabled
rules.explanation: AppArmor profiles define which resources applications may access.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary by site. Some sites may require a policy more restrictive than the default, which is entirely acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that any policies present on the system are enabled.

rules.title: All AppArmor Profiles are enforcing
rules.explanation: AppArmor profiles define which resources applications may access.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Bootloader password is set
rules.scope: Parameters net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*
rules.explanation: A GRUB bootloader password restricts unauthorized modification of boot parameters and menu entries before the operating system starts.
rules.impact: Without a bootloader password, an attacker with physical console access can alter boot parameters (for example to obtain a root shell) and bypass normal authentication.

rules.title: A bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password will require anyone rebooting the system to enter a password before setting boot parameters from the command line.
rules.impact: Requiring a bootloader password at startup will prevent unauthorized entry of boot parameters or modification of the boot partition by an unauthorized user. This prevents weakening of user security (for example, disabling SELinux at boot).

rules.title: XD/NX support is enabled
rules.explanation: Recent x86-family processors support the ability to prevent code execution on a per-memory-page basis. On AMD processors this capability is typically called No Execute (NX), and on Intel processors it is called Execute Disable (XD). This capability can help prevent exploitation of buffer overflow vulnerabilities and should be enabled whenever possible. Additional steps must be taken to ensure that this protection is enabled, especially on 32-bit systems. Other processors, such as Itanium and POWER, include such support from the start, and the standard kernel for those platforms supports this feature.
rules.impact: Enabling any feature that can protect against buffer overflow attacks improves system security.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit-mitigation technique that randomly arranges the address space of key process data areas.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory region placement makes memory-page exploits harder to write because memory layout continually changes.

rules.title: Prelinking is disabled
rules.explanation: prelink is a program that modifies ELF shared libraries and dynamically linked ELF binaries so that the time required for the dynamic linker to perform relocations at startup is significantly reduced.
rules.impact: The prelink feature can interfere with AIDE because it modifies binary files. Prelinking can also increase system vulnerability if a malicious user is able to compromise a shared library such as libc.

rules.title: Core dumps are restricted
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program was aborted. It can also be used to collect sensitive information from the core file. The system provides the ability to set a soft limit for core dumps, but it can be changed by the user.
rules.impact: Setting a hard limit for core dumps prevents users from overriding the soft limit. If core dumps are required, consider setting limits for user groups (see limits.conf(5)). In addition, setting the fs.suid_dumpable variable to 0 will prevent setuid programs from dumping core.

rules.title: Automatic error reporting is disabled
rules.explanation: The Apport error reporting service automatically creates crash reports for debugging.
rules.impact: Apport collects potentially sensitive data such as memory dumps, stack traces, and log files. These may contain passwords, credit-card numbers, serial numbers, and other private material.

rules.title: /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd banner is shown to every user who logs in. It must carry the authorisation warning and must not disclose the operating system release.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue banner is shown to every user who logs in. It must carry the authorisation warning and must not disclose the operating system release.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net banner is shown to every user who logs in. It must carry the authorisation warning and must not disclose the operating system release.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file should be owned by root with mode 0644 or more restrictive so that unprivileged users cannot modify the post-login message.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have the correct access settings, it can be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before logon on local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have the correct access settings, it can be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue.net does not have the correct access configuration, it can be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly /etc/motd
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and function as a message of the day for authenticated users. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log in on local terminals. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information may be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured services. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at logon. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following parameters, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Remote banner disclosure of OS details assists reconnaissance before authentication and can undermine the legal and policy value of an authorized-use notice.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/motd are configured
rules.explanation: These files define users, groups, passwords and shells. Excess permissions let an unprivileged user read or replace them and take over the host.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/issue are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on to local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: GDM automatic mounting of removable media is disabled
rules.impact: Automatic mounting of removable media can pose a security threat because it may allow malicious code to execute automatically when media is connected.
rules.explanation: The setting is turned off so that the feature it enables cannot be used against the host.

rules.title: GDM disabling automatic mounting of removable media is not overridden
rules.impact: Preventing override of this setting ensures that the security policy prohibiting automounting remains enforced.
rules.explanation: GNOME is prevented from mounting removable media automatically so that untrusted filesystems are not attached without the user asking for it.

rules.title: Autorun is never enabled in GDM
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that AutoPlay for removable media is never permitted in GDM.
rules.impact: Disabling autorun prevents automatic execution of code from removable media, a common malware attack vector.

rules.title: Autorun is never overridden in GDM
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the autorun-never setting cannot be overridden by the user.
rules.impact: Preventing override ensures that the AutoPlay restriction policy remains enforced for all users.

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: XDMCP (X Display Manager Control Protocol) enables remote graphical display-manager access. It is an older protocol with weak security properties compared with modern remote-access methods.
rules.impact: Enabled XDMCP expands remote attack surface for graphical sessions and can expose display-manager services over the network without modern encryption and authentication.

rules.title: Autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs automatically mounts filesystems on demand when paths are accessed. It is used for on-demand mounting of local or network filesystems.
rules.impact: If on-demand automounting is not required, retaining autofs increases the attack surface and may allow unintended mounting of network or local resources.

rules.title: The X Window System is not installed
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface (GUI) in which users can have multiple windows in which to run programs and various add-ons. The X Window System is typically used on workstations where users log on, but not on servers where users typically do not log on using a graphical interface.
rules.impact: If your organization does not require graphical login via X Windows, remove it to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The Avahi server is not enabled
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a system for multicast DNS/DNS-SD service discovery. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on a local network without a specific configuration. For example, a user can connect a computer to the network and Avahi will automatically find printers to print to, files to browse, people to communicate with, and network services running on the machine.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is generally not required for system functionality. It is recommended to disable the service to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: See section 2.2.4 in CentOS Linux 7 v3.1.2 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: CUPS is not enabled
rules.explanation: The Common Unix Printing System (CUPS) allows printing to both local and network printers. A system running CUPS can also accept print jobs from remote systems and print them on local printers. It also provides the ability to administer the service remotely over the web.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to print jobs or accept print jobs from other systems, it is recommended to disable CUPS to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The DHCP server is not enabled
rules.explanation: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a service that allows machines to be assigned IP addresses dynamically.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically configured to operate as a DHCP server, it is recommended to disable this service to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The LDAP server is not enabled
rules.explanation: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a method for looking up information from a central database.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP server, it is recommended to disable the software to reduce the potential attack likelihood.

rules.title: NFS and RPC are not enabled
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most common file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides the ability for systems to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not export NFS shares or act as an NFS client, it is recommended to disable these services to reduce the likelihood of a remote attack.

rules.title: Message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Message access server services (for example, IMAP, POP3) are used to access electronic mail.
rules.impact: If the system is not functioning as a mail server, these services should not be running in order to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The FTP server is not enabled
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows networked computers to transfer files between a server and clients over a network where authentication is absent (disallow anonymous user connections to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or credentials. It is recommended to use sftp if file transfer is required. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The HTTP server is not enabled
rules.explanation: HTTP or web servers provide the ability to host website content.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a web server, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Unused IMAP and POP3 server is not disabled
rules.explanation: dovecot is an open-source IMAP and POP3 server for Linux-based systems used by default.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Samba is not enabled
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise filesystems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and filesystems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this service can be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The HTTP proxy server is not enabled
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: If a proxy server is not required, it is recommended to disable the squid proxy to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The SNMP server is not enabled
rules.explanation: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP, execute commands, or collect information and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: An SNMP server can communicate using SNMP v1, which transmits data in the clear and does not require authentication to execute commands. If at all possible, it is recommended that the SNMP service not be used. If SNMP is required, the server should be configured to prohibit the use of SNMP v1.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs), such as sendmail and Postfix, are used to listen for incoming mail and deliver messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If a mail server is not used on the system, it is recommended that the MTA be configured to process local mail only.
rules.impact: The MTA daemon should not listen on a port unless the server is intended to be a mail server that receives and processes mail from other systems.

rules.title: The rsync service is not enabled
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service is used to synchronize files between systems over network channels.
rules.impact: The rsyncd service presents a security threat because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.

rules.title: The NIS server is not enabled
rules.explanation: Network Information Service (NIS) (formerly known as "Yellow Pages") is a client-server directory service protocol for distributing system configuration files.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers such as Apache and Nginx serve HTTP/HTTPS content. Hosts that are not designated web servers should not run these services.
rules.impact: Unnecessary web servers expand the network attack surface and may expose internal content or web application vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: Xinetd is an enhanced super-server that manages other services based on incoming requests.
rules.impact: xinetd can manage many services and increases the attack surface. If it is not used, it should be disabled.

rules.title: X window server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An X Window System server provides graphical display services. Production servers typically do not require a local graphical environment.
rules.impact: Removing unused X Window System components reduces a complex local attack surface and avoids unnecessary graphical-session exposure on servers.

rules.title: Mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: A mail transfer agent (MTA) such as Postfix relays and delivers email. Binding the MTA to localhost restricts it to local delivery rather than accepting network mail.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be abused as an open relay and exposes mail-protocol attack surface on hosts that should only send local mail.

rules.title: Only approved services are listening on a network interface
rules.explanation: Every listening socket is an entry point. The host must expose only the services the baseline approves, on the interfaces and ports they are meant to use.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The NIS client is not installed
rules.explanation: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks and buffer overflows and has weak authentication for NIS map queries. NIS is typically replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended that the service be removed.
rules.impact: NIS client use can expose credential material on the network. Removing unused NIS clients reduces reliance on insecure legacy authentication infrastructure.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: The rsh package contains client commands for rsh services.
rules.impact: These legacy clients contain numerous vulnerabilities and have been replaced by the more secure SSH package. Even if the server is removed, it is best to ensure that the client is also removed to prevent users from accidentally using these commands

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: Messaging software allows users to send and receive messages across systems via a terminal session. A talk client that can initiate talk sessions is installed by default.
rules.impact: The software poses a security risk because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Use of unencrypted MEDIUM transmission may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP client utilities (such as ldap-utils) query directory services. Hosts that do not need to query LDAP typically do not require these tools.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended that the software be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Rpcbind is removed
rules.explanation: Remote Procedure Call (RPC) is a method for creating low-level client-server applications across different system architectures. This requires an RPC-compatible client to listen on a network port. The helper package is rpcbind.
rules.impact: If RPC is not required, it is recommended to remove this service to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that only one time synchronization daemon is running on the system (for example, systemd-timesyncd or chrony).
rules.impact: Having multiple time-synchronization daemons can lead to conflicts and incorrect time configuration. Using a single daemon ensures consistency and simplifies management.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is configured with authorized time servers
rules.explanation: systemd-timesyncd synchronizes system time using configured NTP sources. Authorized organizational time servers should be specified when timesyncd is used.
rules.impact: Synchronization with unauthorized NTP sources can allow manipulation of system time, affecting authentication, logging, and certificate validity.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When systemd-timesyncd is the selected time-synchronization client, it should be enabled at boot and actively running.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Chrony is configured with authorized time servers
rules.explanation: Chrony synchronizes system time using NTP sources. The server and pool directives identify authorized time servers or pools.
rules.impact: Proper chrony configuration with authorized sources helps maintain accurate time for security protocols and consistent enterprise-wide log timestamps.

rules.title: Chrony runs as the _chrony user
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the chrony daemon runs as the dedicated unprivileged user _chrony.
rules.impact: Running services as unprivileged users reduces potential damage if a service is compromised (principle of least privilege).

rules.title: Chrony is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When chrony is the selected time-synchronization client, chronyd should be enabled at boot and actively running.
rules.impact: A non-running chrony client allows clock drift that can disrupt authentication, certificate validation, and forensic log correlation.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon executes scheduled jobs for system maintenance and administrative tasks according to crontab schedules.
rules.impact: An inactive cron daemon may prevent timely execution of security-related maintenance such as log rotation and integrity checks.

rules.impact: Restricting access to crontab prevents unauthorized creation or modification of cron jobs by users.

rules.explanation: at holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: IPv6 status is identified
rules.explanation: If IPv6 is not required it is disabled; if it is required, its parameters are hardened the same way as the IPv4 ones. Knowing which case applies is a prerequisite for the rest of the network checks.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Wi-Fi is disabled on the OS
rules.explanation: The operating system includes a set of wireless networking tools that allow system administrators to configure and use wireless networks
rules.impact: If wireless communication is not used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce a potential attack vector.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth services provide wireless connectivity to peripheral devices.
rules.impact: If Bluetooth is not required, it should be disabled to reduce the attack surface and prevent potential Bluetooth-based attacks.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects to another router in an attempt to disrupt routing and give users access to a system configured by the attacker rather than a legitimate system.
rules.explanation: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol rarely required in typical server environments.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.impact: Setting the flag to 0 ensures that a multi-interface system can never forward packets and therefore will never serve as a router.
rules.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol that supports message-oriented communication with multiple streams in a single association.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) is a protocol used in some high-performance clustered environments.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling RDS when it is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication) is a protocol used by some clustered applications for inter-node messaging.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling TIPC when cluster software does not require it reduces that exposure.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: In a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. Conversely, packets that are not source-routed follow a path determined by routers on the network. In some cases, systems may not be routable or reachable from certain locations (for example, private addresses versus Internet-routable addresses), and source-routed packets would therefore need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system's acceptance of source-routed packets. If source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to the system's private addresses because a route can be specified rather than relying on routing protocols that would not permit that routing.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host information for sending packets via an alternate path. This is a way to update your system's routing tables from outside. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.
rules.impact: Attackers can use forged ICMP redirect messages to maliciously alter system routing tables and cause them to send packets to the wrong networks and allow captured system packets.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are likely to be trusted.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table updates from possibly compromised known gateways.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged
rules.explanation: When this feature is enabled, it logs packets with non-routable source addresses in the kernel log.
rules.impact: Enabling this feature and logging these packets allows an administrator to investigate the likelihood that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system under investigation.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 1 will cause the system to ignore all ICMP echo requests and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo requests and timestamps with broadcast or multicast destinations for your network can be used to cause your host to start (or participate in) a Smurf attack. A Smurf attack is based on an attacker sending a large number of ICMP messages with a spoofed source address. All hosts that receive this message and respond will send echo reply messages back to the spoofed address, which is likely not routable. If many hosts respond to the packets, the volume of traffic on the network can multiply significantly.

rules.title: Logging of bogus responses by the kernel is prevented
rules.explanation: Setting icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses to 1 prevents the kernel from logging bogus (RFC-1122-incompatible) responses to broadcast frames, preventing file systems from being filled with useless log messages.
rules.impact: Some routers (and some attackers) will send replies that violate RFC-1122 and attempt to fill the log filesystem with a large number of useless error messages.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 causes the Linux kernel to use reverse-path filtering on a received packet to determine whether the packet is valid. Essentially, with reverse-path filtering, if the return packet would not leave through the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting these flags is a good way to deter attackers from sending packets into your system that cannot be answered. However, this feature fails if asymmetric routing is used. That occurs when dynamic routing protocols (BGP, OSPF, etc.) are used on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
rules.explanation: When the tcp_syncookies parameter is set, the kernel will process TCP SYN packets normally until the connection queue is full. At that point the SYN cookie feature is triggered, which does not use the SYN queue. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN|ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses and port numbers, as well as the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to accept the connection even if there is no matching SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN attacks for denial of service; the targeted system receives many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This quickly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents legitimate connections. SYN cookies allow the system to accept valid connections even while it is under a denial-of-service attack.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: This setting disables the system's ability to accept IPv6 router advertisements.
rules.impact: It is recommended that systems not accept router advertisements, as they can be tricked into routing traffic to compromised machines. Setting static routes on the system (typically a single default route to a trusted router) protects the system from incorrect routes.

rules.title: Tcp syn cookies is enabled
rules.explanation: TCP SYN cookies allow a server to validate new TCP connections under SYN flood conditions without retaining full connection state for every SYN.
rules.impact: Without SYN cookies, SYN flood attacks can exhaust incomplete-connection tables and deny new legitimate connections.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: IPv6 Router Advertisements (RA) advertise default routers and prefixes used for address autoconfiguration on a link.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited RAs can allow attackers to inject rogue IPv6 routers and redirect traffic, including on hosts primarily using IPv4.

rules.title: A single firewall configuration utility is in use
rules.explanation: Host firewall policy may be managed by UFW, nftables, or iptables tooling. Using multiple managers concurrently can produce conflicting rulesets.
rules.impact: Conflicting firewall managers create unpredictable filtering behavior and can leave unintended gaps or block legitimate traffic.

rules.title: UFW is installed
rules.explanation: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is Ubuntu's frontend for managing host firewall rules. Installation is required when UFW is the chosen firewall utility.
rules.impact: Without a host firewall utility, inbound network services lack a consistent local filtering policy and may be reachable more broadly than intended.

rules.title: Nftables is not in use with ufw
rules.explanation: A single host firewall implementation is expected, with a default deny policy, loopback traffic allowed and a rule set that is loaded at boot. Mixing ufw, nftables and iptables produces rules whose evaluation order is hard to reason about.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Iptables-persistent is not installed with ufw
rules.explanation: iptables-persistent and UFW both manage persistence of iptables-based rules. Installing both can cause conflicting restore behavior at boot.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: UFW service is enabled
rules.explanation: The UFW service applies configured firewall rules and should be enabled so filtering remains active across reboots.
rules.impact: A disabled UFW service means configured rules are not enforced, leaving network ports reachable according to default kernel networking behavior.

rules.title: UFW loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: UFW should allow traffic on the loopback interface required for local inter-process communication, while blocking spoofed loopback addresses arriving on other interfaces.
rules.impact: Incorrect loopback handling can break local services or allow spoofed 127.0.0.0/8 addresses to bypass intended access controls.

rules.title: UFW outbound connections are configured
rules.explanation: Configure firewall rules for new outbound connections. Note: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system. • Unlike iptables, when a new outbound rule is added, ufw automatically handles related established connections, so no rules for the latter type are required.
rules.impact: If rules for new outbound connections are missing, all packets will be dropped by the default policy, preventing network use.

rules.title: UFW firewall rules exist for all open ports
rules.explanation: Services and ports can be allowed or explicitly denied. Note: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system. • The remediation command opens the port to traffic from all sources. Review the ufw documentation and apply any restrictions in accordance with site policy.
rules.impact: To reduce the system's attack surface, all services and ports should be blocked unless they are required. • Any ports open on non-loopback addresses need firewall rules to control traffic. • If a firewall rule is not configured for open ports, the default firewall policy will drop all packets to those ports. • For required ports, a firewall rule should be created that allows approved connections according to local site policy. • For unapproved ports, an explicit deny rule should be created.

rules.title: UFW default deny firewall policy
rules.explanation: A default-deny connection policy ensures that any unconfigured network use is rejected. Note: Any port or protocol without an explicit allow before the default deny will be blocked.

rules.title: Nftables is installed

rules.impact: When nftables is the chosen firewall backend, the packages must be present so filtering rules can be defined and enforced.

rules.title: UFW is uninstalled or disabled with nftables

rules.title: An nftables table exists

rules.impact: Without a configured table, nftables cannot enforce host packet filtering for inbound or forwarded traffic.

rules.title: Nftables base chains exist

rules.impact: If a base chain with a hook for input, forward, and drop does not exist, packets that would pass through these chains will not be affected by nftables.

rules.explanation: The cron daemon is used to run batch jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that needs to run. If another task-scheduling method is not used, cron is used to run them and should be enabled and running.

rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to manage its own jobs. The commands in this item ensure that root is the user and group owner of the file, and that only the owner can access the file.

rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that should run similarly to hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but require more granular control of their execution. rules.title: Access to /cron is permitted only for authorized users
