rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication trusts remote hosts based on host identity rather than verifying individual users with keys or passwords.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: IgnoreRhosts causes sshd to ignore .rhosts and .shosts files as authentication sources. Those legacy trust files are insecure by modern standards.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: The KexAlgorithms offered by sshd are restricted to the modern set so that weak or deprecated cryptography cannot be negotiated with the server.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime limits how long an unauthenticated SSH connection may remain open while authentication is attempted.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: The sshd LogLevel setting controls the detail of authentication and session events written to logs (commonly VERBOSE or INFO).
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH MACs are configured
rules.explanation: The MACs offered by sshd are restricted to the modern set so that weak or deprecated cryptography cannot be negotiated with the server.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of multiplexed sessions that may be opened over a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits concurrent unauthenticated SSH connections, protecting the daemon from connection floods before authentication completes.
rules.impact: Without MaxStartups limits, attackers can exhaust SSH connection capacity and deny remote administrative access.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitEmptyPasswords controls whether accounts with empty password strings may authenticate over SSH.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account may authenticate directly over SSH. Administrative access is preferably obtained via individual accounts and privilege elevation.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables through files such as ~/.ssh/environment that sshd will apply at login.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: UsePAM causes sshd to authenticate and establish sessions through the PAM stack, integrating password policy, account locks, and related controls.
rules.impact: Disabling UsePAM bypasses PAM-based password policy, lockout, and multifactor controls for SSH authentication.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo is the standard mechanism for controlled privilege elevation, allowing authorized users to run specific commands as another user while recording activity.
rules.impact: Without sudo, administrators often share direct root logins, reducing accountability and fine-grained privilege separation.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: The sudo use_pty option forces commands run through sudo to execute in a pseudo-terminal.
rules.impact: Requiring a pty reduces certain classes of abuse involving backgrounded or redirected privileged processes after a sudo invocation.

rules.title: Sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: sudo can use its own log file
rules.impact: The sudo log file simplifies auditing of sudo commands.

rules.title: Users must provide a password to elevate privileges
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that users must enter their password when using sudo to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Requiring a password provides an additional authentication check and prevents unauthorized privilege elevation if a user session is left unattended.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the global setting that disables re-authentication for privilege elevation is not set.
rules.impact: Re-authentication ensures that the user is still present and authorized when executing privileged commands, which improves security.

rules.title: Sudo authentication timeout is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the sudo authentication timeout (the period during which a user can execute sudo commands without re-entering a password) is configured to a reasonable value.
rules.impact: Configuring an authentication timeout limits how long a sudo session remains active without re-authentication, reducing risk if the session is hijacked.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in the /etc/pam.d/su file, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead allows system administrators to better control user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: The latest version of pam is installed
rules.explanation: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) is the authentication framework used on Linux.
rules.impact: Installing the latest version of PAM ensures the latest security patches and feature improvements are present.

rules.title: The latest version of libpam-modules is installed
rules.explanation: The libpam-modules library contains PAM modules used for authentication.
rules.impact: Updating libpam-modules ensures that the latest modules and security patches are used for authentication.

rules.title: The latest version of libpam-pwquality is installed
rules.explanation: The libpam-pwquality library provides a PAM module for password complexity checking.
rules.impact: Updating libpam-pwquality ensures that the latest password complexity checking features and security fixes are available.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_unix module is used for standard Unix authentication (password verification via /etc/shadow).
rules.impact: Enabling pam_unix ensures that the system can perform basic user authentication using local accounts.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock module locks an account after several failed logon attempts.
rules.impact: Enabling pam_faillock helps prevent password brute-force attacks by temporarily locking accounts after authentication failures.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality module enforces password complexity when passwords are set or changed.
rules.impact: Enabling pam_pwquality enforces password complexity policies, which improves overall account security.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_swhistory module (sometimes pam_pwhistory) tracks a user's password history to prevent reuse of old passwords.
rules.impact: Enabling pam_swhistory helps enforce password history policies, preventing reuse of recently used passwords.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that account lockout after multiple failed password attempts is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring lockout after failed attempts mitigates password brute-force attacks, making it more difficult for attackers to guess passwords.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the account lockout duration after lockout (that is, how long the account remains locked) is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring an unlock time provides a balance between security and usability by automatically unlocking accounts after a defined period.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts includes the root account
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the lockout policy after failed password attempts also applies to the root account.
rules.impact: Including the root account in the lockout policy prevents password brute-force attacks against the most privileged account.

rules.title: The number of changed password characters is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that a minimum number of characters must be changed relative to the old password when a password is changed.
rules.impact: This prevents trivial password changes (for example, appending a digit), improving security by ensuring a genuine password change.

rules.title: Minimum password length is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that a minimum password length is set.
rules.impact: Longer passwords are generally more resistant to brute-force attacks. Setting a minimum length is a fundamental password security practice.

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that passwords must meet complexity requirements (for example, contain uppercase and lowercase characters, digits, and special characters).
rules.impact: Complex passwords are harder to guess or crack with brute-force attacks, which increases account security.

rules.title: Consecutive identical password characters are configured
rules.explanation: This requirement limits the number of identical consecutive characters in a password.
rules.impact: Restricting repeated characters prevents use of simple, easily guessed passwords such as "aaaaaa".

rules.title: The maximum number of consecutive password characters is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement limits the number of sequential characters (for example, "abcde" or "12345") in a password.
rules.impact: Restricting consecutive characters prevents the use of predictable patterns that can be easily guessed.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that dictionary checking is performed when a password is set, to prevent the use of common words.
rules.impact: Dictionary checking prevents the use of weak passwords based on common words that are easy to guess.

rules.title: Password quality checking is applied
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that password quality checking (combining parameters such as length, complexity, etc.) is enforced.
rules.impact: Enforcing quality checking ensures that all new passwords comply with the organization's security policy.

rules.title: Password quality is applied for the root user
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that password quality checking is also applied to the root account.
rules.impact: The root account is the most privileged, so it is especially important that its password is strong and complies with the complexity policy.

rules.title: Password history is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the system remembers a defined number of a user's previous passwords and prevents their reuse.
rules.impact: Enforcing password history prevents cycling through a small set of passwords, which improves security.

rules.title: Password history is applied for the root user
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the password history policy is applied to the root account.
rules.impact: Applying password history to root prevents reuse of old passwords for the most critical account.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the pam_swhistory module uses the use_authtok parameter to obtain the new password from the previous PAM module.
rules.impact: Using use_authtok ensures that the new password is correctly passed between PAM modules in the authentication stack.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the pam_unix module does not contain the nullok parameter, which permits empty passwords.
rules.impact: Removing nullok prevents logon to accounts with empty passwords, which is a serious security weakness.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the pam_unix module does not contain the remember parameter (password history is managed by pam_swhistory).
rules.impact: Password history functionality should be managed by a dedicated module (pam_swhistory), not pam_unix, for clarity and correct operation.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that pam_unix is configured to use a strong password hashing algorithm (for example, yescrypt, sha512).
rules.impact: Using a strong hashing algorithm protects password hashes from brute-force attacks if the /etc/shadow file is compromised.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the pam_unix module uses the use_authtok parameter to obtain the new password from the previous PAM module (for example, from pam_pwquality).
rules.impact: Using use_authtok ensures that pam_unix uses the already validated and possibly modified password from the previous module, providing consistency.

rules.title: Password expiration is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the maximum lifetime of a password before it must be changed.
rules.impact: Unbounded password lifetime allows compromised credentials to remain valid indefinitely without forced rotation.

rules.title: Minimum password days is configured
rules.explanation: Password ageing and quality settings are enforced through the PAM stack and /etc/login.defs. Weak or unmanaged passwords are the most common way into a host.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs defines how many days before expiration users are warned to change their passwords.
rules.impact: Adequate warning reduces abrupt lockouts and unsafe ad-hoc recovery practices when passwords expire unexpectedly.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs selects the default hashing algorithm used when new local passwords are created.
rules.impact: Strong hashing algorithms increase the cost of offline cracking if password hashes are obtained from the system.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE in /etc/login.defs defines how many days after password expiration an account is locked if the password is not changed.
rules.impact: Locking inactive expired accounts reduces the risk that abandoned credentials remain usable after expiration.

rules.title: All users last password change date is in the past
rules.explanation: Accounts whose password change date is in the future bypass expiry. The shadow aging fields must reflect a real last change for every interactive account.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: UID 0 confers unrestricted superuser privileges. Only the root account should have UID 0.
rules.impact: Additional UID 0 accounts provide equivalent root access that can bypass monitoring focused on the root username.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that only the root account has group identifier (GID) 0.
rules.impact: GID 0 is typically associated with the root group. Other accounts with GID 0 can cause confusion and potential access-control issues.

rules.title: The root group is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that only the root group has group identifier (GID) 0.
rules.impact: Having multiple groups with GID 0 can cause confusion in permission management and potential vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Access to the root account is controlled
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that access to the root account is controlled (for example, allowed only via sudo or directly from specific terminals).
rules.impact: Restricting direct root access reduces the risk of compromise of the most privileged account and encourages use of auditable privilege-elevation methods (sudo).

rules.title: Root path integrity
rules.explanation: The PATH of root must not contain writable directories or "." so that a command run by root cannot be replaced by an unprivileged user.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that umask (the default file-creation mask) for the root user is set to a secure value (for example, 022 or 027).
rules.impact: A secure root umask ensures that new files and directories created by root do not have overly permissive permissions by default.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that system accounts (for example, daemon, bin) have a login shell specified in /etc/passwd that does not allow interactive login (for example, /usr/sbin/nologin).
rules.impact: Preventing interactive logon for system accounts reduces the risk of an attacker using them to obtain shell access.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that accounts without a valid login shell are locked (for example, the password is locked in /etc/shadow).
rules.impact: Locking such accounts adds an extra layer of security by preventing any possibility of authentication with them.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that /usr/sbin/nologin (or a similar shell that denies login) is not listed in the /etc/shells file.
rules.impact: The /etc/shells file contains the list of valid login shells. Including nologin in this list can cause unexpected behavior, because nologin is intended to deny login.

rules.title: Default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT setting defines an idle timeout after which interactive shells automatically exit.
rules.impact: Idle shell timeouts reduce the window during which an unattended terminal session can be abused without re-authentication.

rules.title: Default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: A default umask in global shell profiles sets creation permissions for files and directories created by interactive users.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask (such as 022) creates world-readable files by default, increasing the chance of accidental data exposure.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) builds a database of file attributes and hashes to detect unauthorized filesystem changes.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Configure permissions for /etc/passwd
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user-account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for those utilities to function.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Configure permissions for /etc/passwd-
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: The journald service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journald service (for log management) is enabled and active.
rules.impact: systemd (journald) logs are a key component for recording system events. Their operation is necessary for auditing and troubleshooting.

rules.title: Access to the log file is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that access permissions on systemd-journald log files are configured correctly (for example, readable only by root and the systemd-journal group).
rules.impact: Proper permission configuration protects logs from unauthorized reading or modification, preserving their confidentiality and integrity.

rules.title: Log file rotation is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that rotation (archiving and deletion of old records) of systemd-journald log files is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring rotation prevents log files from exhausting disk space and controls log retention duration.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-remote package is installed if remote log forwarding is required.
rules.impact: systemd-journal-remote allows logs to be sent to a remote server for centralized collection, which improves security and manageability.
rules.scope: See section 5.1.2.1.1 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload authentication is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that authentication for systemd-journal-upload (sending logs to a remote server) is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring authentication prevents unauthorized submission of logs or submission to spoofed servers.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-upload service is enabled and active when remote log forwarding is used.
rules.impact: Enabling the service is required to actually send logs to the remote host.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the systemd-journal-remote service (for receiving logs from remote hosts) is not used if it is not needed.
rules.impact: If the system is not intended to receive remote logs, disabling this service reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: ForwardToSyslog logging is disabled
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the ForwardToSyslog parameter in the journald configuration is disabled if syslog is not used to receive logs.
rules.impact: Disabling unnecessary forwarding simplifies logging configuration and prevents potential log loss or duplication.

rules.title: Journald compression is configured
rules.explanation: journald can compress stored journal data to reduce disk usage while retaining more history within available space.
rules.impact: Compression helps sustain longer retention for retrospective investigation when disk capacity is limited.

rules.title: Journald Storage is configured
rules.explanation: System logs must be collected, rotated and kept in files no unprivileged user can modify. Without them, an intrusion cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the syslog service (for example, rsyslog) is enabled and active if it is used for logging.
rules.impact: An active syslog service is required to collect, process, and store system and application event logs.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the syslog package (for example, rsyslog) is installed if traditional syslog logging is required.
rules.impact: Installing the package provides syslog functionality for log management.

rules.title: Journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that journald is configured to forward logs to syslog if a combined logging system is used.
rules.impact: This provides compatibility with applications or processes that expect logs in the traditional syslog format.

rules.title: Rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the syslog log file creation mode (permissions for new log files) is configured securely (for example, 640).
rules.impact: Secure permissions on log files protect sensitive information in the logs from unauthorized reading.

rules.title: Rsyslog logging is configured
rules.explanation: System logs must be collected, rotated and kept in files no unprivileged user can modify. Without them, an intrusion cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: System logs must be collected, rotated and kept in files no unprivileged user can modify. Without them, an intrusion cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to accept logs from a remote client
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the syslog service is not configured to accept logs from remote clients unless required.
rules.impact: Disabling remote log reception when it is not needed reduces the network attack surface.

rules.title: Logrotate is configured
rules.explanation: System logs must be collected, rotated and kept in files no unprivileged user can modify. Without them, an intrusion cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Access to all log files has been configured
rules.explanation: Log files are owned by root with restrictive modes so that an intruder cannot erase or rewrite the evidence of their own activity.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux Audit subsystem, which records security-relevant events based on kernel audit rules.
rules.impact: Without audit packages, kernel-level security event collection required for many compliance and investigation use cases is unavailable.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd service must be enabled and running so audit rules remain loaded and events are written continuously.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd daemon leaves the system without active audit logging of privileged and security-relevant activity.

rules.title: Auditing for processes that start before auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel audit=1 parameter enables auditing early in boot so events that occur before auditd starts can still be captured.
rules.impact: Without early audit enablement, initialization activity may go unrecorded, reducing visibility into pre-auditd compromise techniques.

rules.title: audit_backlog_limit is configured
rules.explanation: Audit records are only useful if the backlog is large enough and the log storage is sized so that records are not lost between rotations.
rules.impact: Missing audit records make tampering hard to prove and often go unnoticed until an incident review.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: max_log_file sets the maximum size of individual audit log files before rotation or other configured actions occur.
rules.impact: Appropriate log size settings help balance retention needs against the risk of filling the audit filesystem.

rules.title: Audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: max_log_file_action settings such as keep_logs retain old audit logs rather than deleting them automatically when size limits are reached.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs can destroy evidence needed for investigations and compliance retention.

rules.title: System is disabled when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: When the audit log is full the system must stop rather than drop records. Losing audit data silently defeats the purpose of auditing.
rules.impact: Missing audit records make tampering hard to prove and often go unnoticed until an incident review.

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs are low on space
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the system warns administrators when audit log space is exhausted.
rules.impact: Timely warning allows administrators to take action (free or increase space) before audit space is exhausted, which could result in loss of audit records.

rules.title: Changes to system administration scope (sudoers) is collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records changes to system administration scope (sudoers). Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: Missing audit records make tampering hard to prove and often go unnoticed until an incident review.

rules.title: Actions on behalf of another user are always logged
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that actions performed on behalf of another user (for example, via sudo or su) are always recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Logging such actions is critical for accountability and for investigating incidents involving privilege escalation or impersonation.

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that events that modify the sudo log file (for example, /var/log/sudo.log) are recorded in the audit.
rules.impact: Protecting the integrity of the sudo log is important because it contains records of privileged actions. Auditing its modifications helps detect tampering.

rules.title: Events that modify date and time information are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records events that modify date and time information. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Events that modify the network environment are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records events that modify the network environment. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records use of privileged commands. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: Unaudited use of privileged commands reduces visibility into privilege-escalation activity on the host.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules can record failed open and similar attempts that return permission errors such as EACCES or EPERM.
rules.impact: Patterns of failed file access often indicate reconnaissance or attempts to reach protected data and should be visible to investigators.

rules.title: Events that modify user/group information are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records events that modify user/group information. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Discretionary access control permission modification events are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records discretionary access control permission modification events. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Successful filesystem mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record successful mount operations that attach local or remote filesystems to the directory tree.
rules.impact: Unaudited mounts can conceal attachment of removable media or network shares used for data theft or malware introduction.

rules.title: Session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Audit monitoring of session databases such as utmp, wtmp, and btmp records login session creation and related state.
rules.impact: Session records are key investigation artifacts; auditing them helps detect tampering intended to hide interactive access.

rules.title: Login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules related to faillog, lastlog, and similar login accounting help capture successful and failed authentication activity.
rules.impact: Without login-event auditing, unauthorized access and password-guessing patterns are harder to detect and reconstruct.

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records file deletion events by users. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: Mass deletion or renaming may indicate anti-forensics, ransomware, or intentional data destruction and should leave an audit trail.

rules.title: Events that modify mandatory access controls are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records events that modify mandatory access controls. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are collected
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command (changing the SELinux security context) are recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing use of chcon helps track changes to SELinux security contexts, which is important for enforcing mandatory access control policy.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are collected
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that successful and unsuccessful uses of the setfacl command (setting file system access control lists) are recorded in the audit logs.
rules.impact: Auditing setfacl helps track changes to extended file permissions (ACLs), which is important for data access control.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are collected
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command (changing ACLs) are recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing chacl (part of the POSIX ACL tools) helps track changes to access control lists.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are collected
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command (modifying user accounts) are recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing usermod is critical for tracking changes to user accounts, such as changes to groups, shell, or UID.

rules.title: Kernel module loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule records kernel module loading unloading and modification. Without it, these events leave no trace once the process has exited.
rules.impact: Missing audit records make tampering hard to prove and often go unnoticed until an incident review.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: Setting the audit enabled flag to immutable (-e 2) prevents audit rule changes until the next reboot.
rules.impact: Immutability limits the ability of an attacker with elevated privileges to disable or weaken auditing before further malicious actions.

rules.title: The running and saved configurations match
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the current (running) configuration of the audit daemon (auditd) matches the configuration stored on disk.
rules.impact: A mismatch may indicate an unauthorized in-memory configuration change or that on-disk changes have not been applied. This is important for audit configuration integrity.

rules.title: Audit log file mode is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the mode (permissions) of audit log files is configured securely (for example, 640 or more restrictive).
rules.impact: Secure permissions protect audit logs from unauthorized reading or modification.

rules.title: The owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the owner of audit log files is set correctly (typically root).
rules.impact: Correct ownership provides control over log files and prevents unauthorized changes to access permissions.

rules.title: Audit log file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the group owner of audit log files is set correctly (for example, root or adm).
rules.impact: A correct owning group allows read access to be granted to specific system services or administrators while maintaining security.

rules.title: The audit log file directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the mode (permissions) of the directory containing audit log files (for example, /var/log/audit) is configured securely (for example, 750).
rules.impact: Secure directory permissions prevent unauthorized enumeration, deletion, or creation of files in the directory.

rules.title: Audit configuration file mode is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the mode of audit configuration files (for example, /etc/audit/auditd.conf, rules) is configured securely (for example, 640).
rules.impact: Protecting configuration files prevents unauthorized changes to audit settings.

rules.title: The owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the owner of audit configuration files is set correctly (typically root).
rules.impact: A correct owner ensures control over the audit configuration.

rules.title: The owning group of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the group owner of audit configuration files is set correctly (for example, root).
rules.impact: A correct group owner helps control read access to the configuration.

rules.title: The audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the mode of audit utilities (for example, auditctl, ausearch, aureport) is configured securely (for example, 755 or 750).
rules.impact: Secure permissions on audit tools prevent unauthorized modification or execution of those tools.

rules.title: The audit tools owner is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the owner of audit utilities is set correctly (typically root).
rules.impact: The correct owner protects the integrity of audit tools.

rules.title: The group owner of audit tools is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that the group owner of audit utilities is set correctly (for example, root).
rules.impact: The correct group owner helps control access to audit tools.

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd- holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.explanation: /etc/group holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.explanation: /etc/group- holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow- holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow- holds authentication material. Restricting its ownership, group and mode keeps unprivileged users from reading or replacing it.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that access to /etc/shells (the list of valid login shells) is configured correctly.
rules.impact: The /etc/shells file is important for security because it defines which shells may be used for login. Unauthorized modification may allow the use of insecure shells.

rules.title: Access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that access to the /etc/security/opasswd file (which stores old password hashes to enforce password history) is configured correctly.
rules.impact: This file contains sensitive information (old password hashes). Unauthorized access can assist brute-force attacks.

rules.title: World writable files and directories are secured
rules.explanation: Files writable by every user, or owned by a UID/GID that no longer exists, are a standard way to plant content that root will later execute or read.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: No files or directories without an owner and a group exist
rules.explanation: Files writable by every user, or owned by a UID/GID that no longer exists, are a standard way to plant content that root will later execute or read.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are reviewed
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for using an SUID or SGID program is to allow users to perform functions (for example, changing a password) that require root privileges.
rules.impact: There are valid reasons for SUID and SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the action in the audit section and check whether system binaries have a checksum that differs from the package checksum. This indicates that the binary may have been replaced.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts should store an 'x' in the /etc/passwd password field and keep actual hashes in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Password hashes in world-readable /etc/passwd are immediately available for offline cracking; shadowing confines hashes to a restricted file.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An empty password field in /etc/shadow lets the account log in without a password.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: A primary group referenced by a passwd entry but missing from /etc/group leaves the user with an undefined group, which breaks file access assumptions.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Shadow group is empty
rules.explanation: The shadow group allows system programs that require access to read /etc/shadow. Users should not be assigned to the shadow group.
rules.impact: All users assigned to the shadow group will be granted read access to /etc/shadow. If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them. Other security information stored in /etc/shadow (for example, expiration dates) may also be useful for compromising additional user accounts.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Duplicate UIDs let two accounts share the same identity, so files and privileges intended for one are silently shared with the other.
rules.impact: Duplicate UIDs cause multiple accounts to share the same identity for access control, undermining accountability and isolation.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Duplicate GIDs let two accounts share the same identity, so files and privileges intended for one are silently shared with the other.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs create ambiguous group rights and can be abused to inherit privileges associated with another group name.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: User names in /etc/passwd should be unique so authentication and auditing consistently refer to one account identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate user names with different UIDs create ambiguity between tools and authentication paths that can bypass intended access policy.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Group names in /etc/group should be unique so membership and permission checks resolve to a single group identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate group names with different GIDs create ambiguity that can be exploited to obtain unintended group privileges.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: Home directories of interactive users exist, are owned by the user and are not readable by other users, so one account cannot inspect another.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Access to local interactive users' dot files is configured
rules.explanation: This requirement ensures that access permissions on configuration files in user home directories (files beginning with a dot, for example .bashrc, .ssh) are configured securely.
rules.impact: These files often contain sensitive settings, keys, or command history. Overly permissive permissions can allow other users to read or modify them, leading to data leakage or privilege escalation.
